title: The Inspection Nobody Logged: U.S. Roadside Data Decisions Before FMCSA Rewrites the Scorecard
summary: New DataQs clocks, a pending SMS overhaul and tighter broker vetting make every roadside inspection a sales issue. What U.S. carriers should decide now.
body_markdown:
The email lands at 6:50 a.m. on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.


It's from the carrier relations team at one of your top three brokers. Polite, short, and bad. Your account is "under review." Two lanes you've run weekly since spring are paused until their vetting team "completes a safety check."


You run safety and compliance for an 85-truck dry van carrier in the Midwest. Mostly contract freight, some brokered loads to keep trucks moving. Your last compliance review was clean. You don't have a conditional rating. You've never had one.


So what changed?


By 8 a.m. you've found it. A vehicle maintenance violation from an inspection three weeks ago, now sitting in your public record. A brake out-of-service write-up you didn't know existed.


(The carrier is illustrative. The rules, numbers and pressures are real.)


## Three weeks earlier, a scale house in Ohio


Here's how it happened. Unit 4417 got waved into a weigh station on a Tuesday afternoon. The inspector ran a Level II walk-around, found a pushrod stroke over the limit on one axle, and put the truck out of service.


Your driver did everything right in the moment. He called a mobile mechanic, got the brake adjusted, got released and delivered a few hours late. Then he folded the inspection report and stuck it in the door pocket.


Nobody in the office ever saw it. Maintenance never wrote a work order to find out why the brake drifted. Dispatch logged the late delivery as "traffic."


You are not unusual. In CVSA's International Roadcheck, held May 12 to 14, 2026, inspectors put 23.5% of the vehicles they examined out of service on Level I, II and V inspections, up from 22.6% in 2025. Brake problems (brake systems plus the 20% defective brakes category) made up 39.1% of all vehicle out-of-service violations.


What that means for you: almost one in four trucks that get a full look gets parked, and brakes are the most likely reason. If you run 85 trucks, it's not a question of whether a report like this exists. It's whether it reaches your desk before it reaches a broker's.


And it did reach the broker first. To understand why, you have to follow the data.


## Why one write-up travels so far


That inspection didn't stay in Ohio. It went into federal records and showed up in FMCSA's Safety Measurement System on the next monthly update.


The scale of that system is hard to picture. FMCSA says in an April 16, 2026 notice that it publishes information on about 3 million inspections and 5 million violations a year. Your one brake write-up is a drop in that ocean. But it's your drop, and every vetting tool on the market can see it.


Under today's method, a violation counts for 24 months. The most recent six months carry triple weight, and each violation gets a severity score from 1 to 10. Your property carrier percentiles are hidden from the public. The inspections and violations underneath them are not.


Here's the part that hurts. Ratings won't save you, because almost nobody has one. Industry analysis of FMCSA data put about 94% of the roughly 690,000 interstate freight carriers eligible for a rating as unrated as of 2021. When the rating is blank, brokers and shippers read the raw inspection history instead.


And brokers are reading harder than they were a year ago. In May 2026 the Supreme Court ruled in *Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II* that state negligent-selection claims against brokers aren't preempted by federal law. Brokers that pick carriers carefully should still be able to defend themselves. But "carefully" now means documented, and a fresh brake out-of-service is exactly the kind of flag a vetting team can't ignore.


What it means for you: your safety record is now part of your sales pitch, whether you put it there or not. The broker who paused your lanes wasn't punishing you. They were protecting themselves with the only data they had.


So your first question isn't how to fix your score. It's whether this violation should be on your record at all.


## The challenge you can actually win


You pull the report and read it line by line.


The brake violation is legitimate. The stroke was over. You're not going to argue with physics.


But there's a second violation on the same report, a lighting defect, written against a trailer number that isn't yours. Your driver was pulling a customer's drop trailer that day, and the inspector keyed in the wrong unit and plate. That one is worth a challenge.


The challenge system just got better. FMCSA's reformed DataQs process went live on Sept. 18, 2026, and the agency said in mid-October that every state now follows it. The first review can't go to the officer who wrote the violation. States have to open a request within a week, decide the first review within 21 days, decide reconsideration within 21 more, and finish a final review within 45 days. They also have to explain their decisions, which should end the one-line denials.


That's a real change. In 2024, DataQs took in 63,548 requests on inspections and violations, per FMCSA's notice. A lot of carriers filed and never heard a reason.


But the burden of proof is still yours, entirely. A request without evidence is a wasted request, and a request with shaky evidence can backfire.


What it means for you:


-


Challenge errors of fact: wrong carrier, wrong unit, a violation that was corrected and withdrawn at the scene, a crash that wasn't preventable.


-


Don't challenge real defects to buy time. You'll lose, and you'll spend credibility you'll need later.


-


File with documents attached on day one: the report, photos, the trailer interchange, the repair invoice.


-


Track the state's clock. If a deadline passes, escalate. The new process gives you that right.


You file the trailer challenge before lunch. Then you look at the bigger problem, which isn't one violation. It's the math that's about to change under you.


## The scorecard is about to change underneath you


Here's what most fleets miss. The way FMCSA counts your violations is in limbo.


In November 2024, the agency approved an overhauled method for the Safety Measurement System. It sorts more than 2,000 violation codes into roughly 100 groups, so one problem written three ways counts once. It replaces the 1 to 10 severity scale with just two weights. Out-of-service violations get a 2. Most everything else gets a 1. It also swaps the old peer groups for "proportionate percentiles," which should stop scores from jumping for reasons that have nothing to do with safety.


That method has never launched. The current SMS still runs version 3.21, updated in May 2026. On Oct. 28, 2026, an FMCSA safety official told an industry conference the agency will put new SMS proposals out for comment in the coming months.


At the same time, FMCSA's regulatory agenda targeted November 2026 for a proposed rule on safety fitness procedures. It could use inspection data more directly to decide whether a carrier is fit to operate, and it may revisit the satisfactory, conditional and unsatisfactory structure. As of this week it's a target on a calendar, not a published proposal.


What it means for you: don't tune your program for the old formula. Every version on the table points the same way. Out-of-service violations matter more. Repeat problems matter more. Recent problems matter more. If you've been comfortable because your violations were spread across low-severity codes, that comfort has an expiration date.


For your fleet, that points straight back at Unit 4417. A brake that drifts out of adjustment once is a write-up. A brake problem that keeps showing up across your fleet is a pattern, and patterns are what every new method is built to find.


## Closing the loop between the scale and the shop


So you stop thinking about the score and start thinking about the gap. The report sat in a door pocket for three weeks. That's the failure.


The next month's data tells you why this matters. In CVSA's Brake Safety Week, Aug. 23 to 29, 2026, inspectors checked 15,528 vehicles and put 2,369 out of service for brake violations, a 15.3% rate. Brakes aren't a one-off. They're the most common way a clean fleet ends up looking careless.


By Wednesday afternoon you've sketched a new rule set on the whiteboard:


-


**Every inspection report reaches the office the same day.** Clean or not. Drivers photograph it and send it before they roll.


-


**An out-of-service report opens a maintenance work order automatically,** tied to the unit, not just the fix that got the truck released.


-


**Each violation gets a disposition within 48 hours:** accept and correct, coach the driver, or challenge with evidence.


-


**Challenges get a tracked deadline** that matches the state's DataQs clock.


-


**Brokers and shippers get a short evidence packet** when they ask: the violation, the root cause, the repair, and the training.


How you set this up depends on what you are.


If you're an asset carrier, the job is closing the loop between driver, shop and safety, so a fix becomes a pattern you can prove went away.


If you're a broker, the job runs the other way. Your vetting rules need to read inspection history in context: one corrected brake violation on a 200-truck fleet isn't the same as three uncorrected ones on a five-truck fleet. Write those rules down, apply them the same way every time, and keep the record. After *Montgomery* , the record is the defense.


If you're a hybrid, you need both, and you need them separate. Your own trucks get the closed loop. The carriers you broker to get the vetting rules. Mixing the two in one spreadsheet is how a hybrid ends up defending the wrong decision.


## Friday, the lanes come back


On Friday morning you send the broker a one-page packet. The brake violation, owned. The root cause: a slack adjuster that maintenance replaced fleet-wide on that tractor series. The driver's report-intake training, dated. The trailer violation, under DataQs review with the state's deadline noted.


The lanes reopen Monday.


Nothing about your trucks changed between Wednesday and Friday. What changed was that you could show what happened, what you did and when.


That's the real takeaway. No two fleets get inspected the same way. Your lanes, your scale houses, your equipment mix and your customers' vetting rules are yours alone. A fleet hauling heavy loads through Ohio and Indiana sees a different set of inspections than a regional reefer fleet in Georgia. The shops that handle this well build their systems around their own reality: inspection statuses that mean something, work orders that open themselves, permissions that keep a violation from getting closed without a disposition, and carrier rules that a broker can explain to a court.


That work isn't glamorous. It's also what keeps a door-pocket report from costing you two lanes the week before a holiday.


## FAQ


### How long does a roadside inspection violation stay on a carrier's SMS record?


A roadside inspection violation counts in FMCSA's Safety Measurement System for 24 months, with the most recent six months weighted most heavily. The underlying inspection stays in federal records longer, and DataQs challenges can be filed up to three years after an inspection.


### What changed in FMCSA's DataQs process in 2026?


FMCSA's reformed DataQs process went live on Sept. 18, 2026, and requires states to route the first review away from the issuing officer, open requests within seven days, and decide reviews on 21-day, 21-day and 45-day clocks with written explanations. The person filing still carries the full burden of proof.


### Has FMCSA's new CSA scoring method launched?


No. As of late November 2026, carriers are still scored under the existing Safety Measurement System (version 3.21), and the overhauled method approved in November 2024 has not launched. FMCSA said in October 2026 it will put new SMS proposals out for public comment.


### Why do brokers care about a carrier's roadside inspections if the carrier has no safety rating?


Because most carriers have no rating, brokers rely on inspection and violation history to judge safety. After the Supreme Court's May 2026 *Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II* decision allowed negligent-selection claims against brokers to proceed under state law, documented, consistent carrier vetting matters more.


### Which roadside violations are most likely to put a truck out of service?


Brake problems are the most common. In CVSA's 2026 International Roadcheck, brake systems and 20% defective brakes together made up 39.1% of vehicle out-of-service violations, followed by tires, cargo securement and lights.
